title: Omni-Models (Entity-Transport Coupling)
damaged_code:
```rust
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, Queryable, Insertable)]
#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]
#[diesel(table_name = users)]
pub struct User {
    #[serde(skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]
    pub id: Option<i32>,
    pub email: String,
    pub password_hash: String, // Leaks to client if serializing directly!
    pub created_at: chrono::NaiveDateTime,
}
```
pattern: Using a single massive struct decorated with database-specific ORM attributes, API serialization tags, and validation rules to represent database storage, business logic, and API network contracts simultaneously.
why_bad: Tightly couples the database schema, API schema, and domain rules. A minor database optimization (like renaming a column) forces a breaking change in the public JSON API. Sensitive fields (like password hashes or internal state variables) can easily leak to external clients if serialization is not manually bypassed.
detection: Look for a single struct decorated with both database ORM attributes (e.g., `#[diesel(...)]`, `#[sqlx(...)]`) and API serialization attributes (e.g., `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]`).
counterexample: Small CRUD-only applications or internal microservices where database schemas and API contracts are guaranteed to be 100% identical and stable.
fix: Decouple the layers. Create separate, dedicated structs for the database representation (`DbUser`), the API wire format (`UserDto`), and the core domain logic (`User`), with explicit mapping conversions.
source: *Martin Fowler - Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002)*, "Data Transfer Object"; *Robert C. Martin - Clean Architecture (2017)*, Chapter 22, "Hexagonal Architecture".
